```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(seqout)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  eval = requireNamespace("genevintage", quietly = TRUE)
)
example_dir <- system.file("extdata", "gene-names", package = "seqout")
read_example <- function(name, ...) {
  read.delim(file.path(example_dir, name), check.names = FALSE, ...)
}
```

`SeqoutGeneNames()` uses the **genevintage** package to change gene IDs to gene names.
`SeqoutCorrectNames()` repairs gene symbols that Excel changed into dates.
The two functions accept the result of `SeqoutMatrix()`.
They also accept a numeric matrix that has one gene in each row.
They do not change the expression values or the order of the rows.
They keep the feature metadata aligned, and they record the original labels and the status of each change.

Install seqout and genevintage from the r-universe of Saket Lab:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("seqout", repos = c(
  "https://saketlab.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"
))
```

The commands for the full data download GEO files and annotation tables when you use them for the first time.
The examples that run in this vignette use small excerpts that seqout includes.
The excerpts have no changes from the original files, and they run offline.
The source URLs and the method of extraction are in
`extdata/gene-names/README.md` in the installed package.

## Old Ensembl IDs from a 2014 single-cell experiment

[GSE52529](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE52529) is the
Monocle study of myoblast differentiation.
It became public on 23 March 2014.
Its single-cell file has 47,192 gene rows and 372 cells.
The rows have the original Ensembl IDs with versions, for example `ENSG00000000003.10`.

The values are FPKM, not raw counts.
Select `GSE52529_fpkm_matrix.txt.gz`.
The `truseq` file is a different file, and it has bulk measurements.

```{r old-study-download, eval=FALSE}
old <- SeqoutListCounts("GSE52529") |>
  SeqoutMatrix(sample = "GSE52529_fpkm_matrix.txt.gz")
dim(old$X)
head(rownames(old$X))

# automatic selection; decision recorded below
automatic <- old |> SeqoutGeneNames()
automatic$gene_annotation[[1]]$annotation
```

The automatic selection of a release is an estimate with a rank.
These conditions can make it incorrect:

*   A filtered set of genes can agree with more than one reference.
*   Two adjacent releases can have the same set of genes.
*   The ID versions do not identify only one annotation.

For this file, the function selects GENCODE 17 on GRCh37.
This agrees with the
[GEO record of the sample](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSM1268960).
It is not necessary to give the release or the assembly.
All 47,192 IDs in the file agree accurately with that reference, and their version suffixes also agree.

```{r automatic-audit, eval=FALSE}
head(SeqoutGeneReport(automatic))
stopifnot(
  identical(unname(old$X), unname(automatic$X)),
  identical(rownames(automatic$X), rownames(automatic$var))
)
```

The rank of the releases does not download an annotation.
It uses the full vector of the original IDs, which seqout includes as a different file from the expression excerpt.
If the rank uses only the genes in the excerpt, the result can be different.

```{r old-study-ranking}
id_file <- gzfile(file.path(example_dir, "GSE52529-gene-ids.txt.gz"))
old_ids <- readLines(id_file)
close(id_file)
head(genevintage::detect_release(old_ids), 3)
```

The example that follows uses the first 12 genes and the first three cells of the file.
It changes the IDs with the related excerpt of GENCODE 17:

```{r old-study-offline}
old_excerpt <- as.matrix(read_example("GSE52529-excerpt.tsv.gz", row.names = 1))
gencode17 <- read_example("gencode17-excerpt.tsv.gz")
old_named <- SeqoutGeneNames(old_excerpt, mapping = gencode17)
SeqoutGeneReport(old_named)[, c("input", "name", "status")]
stopifnot(identical(as.vector(old_excerpt), as.vector(old_named)))
```

The function does not use the version suffixes to find a match.
But the record of changes keeps the suffixes.
For example, `ENSG00000000003.10` becomes `TSPAN6`.

If an ID has no name in the selected annotation, the ID does not change.
If two rows have the same symbol, each row gets a different label.
The `name` column of the record keeps the symbol without the suffix.
The function does not add rows together.

## Repair Excel errors in a real matrix from GEO

[GSE101942](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE101942) has
gene names that Excel changed.
We examined the original file `GSE101942_IPSC_rawCounts.txt.gz`.
It has 56,637 rows and six samples.
Five of the rows are summary rows from the count tool.
The row labels include `1-Mar`, `9-Sep`, and `15-Sep`.

Give the name of the raw-count file to `SeqoutMatrix()`.
The study also has tables of differential expression results, and these tables are not count matrices.

```{r excel-study-download, eval=FALSE}
damaged <- SeqoutListCounts("GSE101942") |>
  SeqoutMatrix(sample = "GSE101942_IPSC_rawCounts.txt.gz")

# explicit target, not automatic
repaired <- damaged |> SeqoutCorrectNames(species = "human", release = 116)
report <- SeqoutGeneReport(repaired)
report[report$status != "unchanged", c("input", "name", "status")]
stopifnot(identical(unname(damaged$X), unname(repaired$X)))
```

With Ensembl 116, the function repairs 25 labels.
`15-Sep` stays unresolved, because this annotation has no candidate for it.

The excerpt in seqout has all the 26 damaged labels.
It also has `TP53` as a control that does not change.
It has the six original sample columns and their counts.
The annotation excerpt has all the candidates in the reference that relate to month names.

```{r excel-study-offline}
excel_excerpt <- as.matrix(read_example("GSE101942-excerpt.tsv.gz", row.names = 1))
human116 <- read_example("ensembl116-excel.tsv.gz")
excel_fixed <- SeqoutCorrectNames(excel_excerpt, mapping = human116, quiet = TRUE)
excel_report <- SeqoutGeneReport(excel_fixed)
excel_report[
  excel_report$input %in% c("1-Mar", "9-Sep", "15-Sep", "TP53"),
  c("input", "name", "status")
]
table(excel_report$status)
stopifnot(identical(as.vector(excel_excerpt), as.vector(excel_fixed)))
```

### Old symbols and new symbols

Human Ensembl 95 and Ensembl 116 give different results for the same damaged labels.
This example compares the two references.
It does not find the release that GSE101942 used.

```{r excel-vintages}
human95 <- read_example("ensembl95-excel.tsv.gz")
excel_old <- SeqoutCorrectNames(excel_excerpt, mapping = human95, quiet = TRUE)
old_report <- SeqoutGeneReport(excel_old)
show <- excel_report$input %in% c("1-Mar", "9-Sep")
data.frame(
  deposited = excel_report$input[show],
  ensembl95 = old_report$name[show],
  ensembl116 = excel_report$name[show]
)
```

With Ensembl 95, `1-Mar` becomes `MARCH1`.
With Ensembl 116, `1-Mar` becomes `MARCHF1`.
With the same references, `9-Sep` becomes `SEPT9` with Ensembl 95 and `SEPTIN9` with Ensembl 116.

The names do not tell seqout the species or the release.
For the repair of Excel errors, you must give an annotation table.
Or, you must give the two arguments `species` and `release`.

The function does not change a date that has more than one candidate.
It gives the status `ambiguous` to that date.
It gives the status `unresolved` to a value that has no candidate.
genevintage cannot repair some formats, and it cannot repair numbers that lost precision.
Before your analysis, examine the report.
Repair only the columns that you know contain gene labels.

If the damaged symbols are in the feature metadata, give that column with the `ids` argument:

```{r feature-column, eval=FALSE}
repaired <- SeqoutCorrectNames(
  rna,
  ids = rna$var$symbol, species = "human", release = 116
)
```

The function keeps the original `var$symbol` column.
The repaired labels become the row names of `X` and of `var`.
Each call adds its record of changes to `gene_annotation`.
To keep this record after you change the data to a Seurat or SingleCellExperiment object,
save the corrected `seqout_matrix`.
